nameStory: This fungus gets its 'sulphureum' name from the Latin word for sulfur, referring to its bright yellow-green color that resembles powdered sulfur. While it doesn't have a widely-used common name, mycologists sometimes call it the 'sulfur trichoderma' for its distinctive sunny hue.
description: Trichoderma sulphureum is a small mold fungus that forms bright yellow-green cushions on decaying wood. These fuzzy patches start out as tiny bumps but can spread to cover several inches of a log surface. The fungus produces masses of microscopic spores that give it a powdery appearance, almost like someone dusted the wood with colored flour. Individual patches are usually less than an inch across but often merge together into larger colonies.

idTips.label: Bright Yellow-Green Color
idTips.description: Look for vivid sulfur-yellow to lime-green patches that almost seem to glow against dark wood - much brighter than most other wood-growing molds

idTips.label: Cushion-Like Growth
idTips.description: Forms dense, rounded cushions that feel slightly spongy when gently pressed - not flat like paint or hard like bracket fungi

idTips.label: Powdery Texture
idTips.description: Surface has a fine, dusty texture that may leave yellow-green powder on your finger if touched lightly

idTips.label: Wood Substrate
idTips.description: Always grows directly on decaying hardwood logs and branches - never on living trees or other surfaces

idTips.label: Size and Pattern
idTips.description: Individual cushions are typically pea-sized to quarter-sized, often clustered together in groups along bark crevices

habitat: Found on decaying hardwood logs and fallen branches in mixed and deciduous forests throughout New England. Prefers well-rotted wood of oak, maple, and birch trees in moist, shaded areas where humidity stays high. Most common in mature forests with plenty of dead wood on the forest floor.

seasonality.spring: Fresh yellow-green cushions begin appearing as temperatures warm and moisture increases from snowmelt and spring rains.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with the most vibrant colors and largest colonies, especially after periods of warm, humid weather.
seasonality.fall: Still active and colorful through autumn, often more noticeable as leaves fall and expose decaying logs.
seasonality.winter: Growth slows dramatically but existing colonies may persist under snow cover, appearing faded and dormant until spring.

funFact: This tiny mold is actually a biological superhero - scientists use Trichoderma species to create eco-friendly pesticides because they naturally attack and destroy harmful plant diseases, essentially farming them as microscopic guardians for crops and gardens.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other bright molds like slime molds or algae, but Trichoderma sulphureum always grows as distinct cushions directly on wood, while slime molds are more irregular and algae appears as flat films. Remember: cushions on wood = Trichoderma.
contextualKnowledge: The genus name 'Trichoderma' means 'hairy skin' in Greek, though you'd need a microscope to see the tiny hair-like structures. Despite being called a mold, this is actually more closely related to cup fungi and morel mushrooms than to household molds.
compareHints: Trichoderma sulphureum stands out from its relatives by its particularly bright yellow-green color - most other Trichoderma species are duller green, white, or orange. Trichoderma viride is similar but tends toward blue-green rather than sulfur-yellow, while the ochre cushion (T. pulvinatum) is distinctly orange-brown rather than yellow-green.
